entities.name: Francesco Carafa di Trajetto
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Francesco Carafa della Spina di Traetto (1773-1818), an Italian cardinal from a preeminent Neapolitan noble family, played a significant role in the tumultuous relationship between the Papacy and the Napoleonic Empire during the early 19th century. His unwavering loyalty to Pope Pius VII amidst Napoleon's ecclesiastical pressures marked him as a figure of principled resistance within the Catholic Church, particularly during a period of profound political upheaval across Europe. Appointed Archbishop of Patras in 1803 and elevated to cardinal by Pius VII later that year, Carafa's early ecclesiastical career was swiftly overshadowed by the escalating conflicts between Napoleon Bonaparte and the Holy See, which tested the fidelity of many high-ranking clergy.

Carafa's most defining period came after Napoleon's annexation of the Papal States in 1809 and the subsequent imprisonment of Pope Pius VII. Like many cardinals who refused to attend Napoleon's second marriage to Marie Louise of Austria in 1810—a union not sanctioned by the Pope—Carafa was stripped of his cardinalatial insignia and banished from Paris. He was then confined by Napoleonic authorities, enduring imprisonment from 1808 until the emperor's downfall in 1815. This period of forced exile and deprivation, shared with thirteen other cardinals collectively known as the "Black Cardinals" due to their forbidden crimson vestments, solidified Carafa's reputation as a staunch defender of papal authority against secular encroachment.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Francesco Carafa di Trajetto's principled resistance as a "Black Cardinal" against Napoleon's ecclesiastical policies exemplified the Catholic Church's struggle for independence, contributing to the post-Napoleonic reassertion of papal authority. His actions reinforced the resolve of the Papacy and the ultramontane movement against state control.
